title: Trace JVM execution with a Hello World Java program
answer: For a simple `HelloWorld` program, the developer writes Java source and the Java compiler (`javac`) compiles that source into a `.class` file containing JVM bytecode. When `java HelloWorld` is executed, the Java launcher starts a JVM, the class loader finds and loads `HelloWorld`, the bytecode verifier checks the class, linking and initialization prepare it, and the JVM invokes `public static void main(String[] args)`. The execution engine interprets bytecode and may JIT-compile frequently executed code into native machine instructions. `System.out.println("Hello World")` ultimately writes the text through the Java runtime to the process output. The JVM also manages runtime memory and other services during execution. The same compatible class bytecode can run on different supported operating systems because each platform provides its own JVM implementation.

steps.title: Create a small JVM learning lab
steps.question: A simple Hello World program is useful because it removes Spring Boot and other framework layers, letting the JVM execution path remain visible. Why should we create this example under AeroTopo's `labs` area instead of replacing or simplifying the real application source?
steps.why: The lab isolates the JVM concept while preserving the real application architecture.

Learning lab isolated ga unte JVM basics clear ga observe cheyyachu, kani real AeroTopo application architecture ni disturb cheyyamu. Full project lo educational artifact ga traceable ga untundi.

steps.title: Auto-type the complete Hello World source
steps.question: The JVM execution story begins with ordinary Java source containing a class and the standard `main` entry point. As IntelliJ types the complete lab program, which source elements will later guide the compiler and JVM toward the statement that prints `Hello World`?

Next stages lo compiler bytecode create chestundi, JVM aa bytecode execute chestundi.

steps.title: Inspect the typed class structure
steps.question: Before compiling, IntelliJ can already understand the class and `main` method structurally because it parses Java source, but that editor understanding is not the same thing as JVM execution. Why is separating IDE code analysis from runtime execution important in this simple example?
steps.why: IDE analysis and JVM execution are different stages with different responsibilities.

steps.title: Open the terminal for the compile-and-run path
steps.question: An IDE Run button can hide several stages that are important when explaining the JVM to a new developer. Why should this lesson use the integrated terminal so the source compilation, bytecode inspection, and JVM launch commands can be observed separately?
steps.why: The terminal exposes the three stages explicitly instead of hiding them behind one IDE button.
steps.why_te: the terminal for the compile-and-run path gurinchi ikkada IDE view tho command-line reality ni compare cheyyadam mukhyam; same project context lo direct verification enduku useful o observe cheyyandi. Terminal lo `javac`, `javap` mariyu `java` stages separate ga visible avutayi. Dini valla source-to-bytecode-to-runtime flow clear ga understand cheyyachu.

steps.title: Compile HelloWorld into a class file
steps.question: Compilation produces the class-file artifact consumed by the JVM. The JVM cannot directly execute the Java source file as the normal compiled-program model being demonstrated here; `javac` first creates JVM bytecode. What does compiling `HelloWorld.java` into `target/lesson15-demo` establish about the artifact that the JVM will load next?
steps.why: Compilation produces the class-file artifact consumed by the JVM.
steps.why_te: Compile HelloWorld into a class file gurinchi ikkada command syntax ni memorize cheyyadam kaadu; terminal output exact ga ye environment leda runtime fact ni prove chestundo evidence laga chudandi. `javac` source ni `HelloWorld.class` bytecode ga compile chestundi. JVM next step lo `.java` text kaakunda ee class-file representation ni load chesi execute chestundi.

steps.title: Inspect the generated JVM bytecode
steps.question: Javap exposes the JVM instruction stream stored in the compiled class file. A `.class` file contains JVM instructions rather than the source statement exactly as written or one operating system's native machine code. Why does inspecting the class with `javap -c` make the platform-independent intermediate bytecode stage easier to understand?
steps.why: Javap exposes the JVM instruction stream stored in the compiled class file.
steps.why_te: the generated JVM bytecode gurinchi ikkada command syntax ni memorize cheyyadam kaadu; terminal output exact ga ye environment leda runtime fact ni prove chestundo evidence laga chudandi. `javap -c` class file lo JVM bytecode instructions ni readable form lo chupistundi. Ee intermediate instruction set host CPU native code kaadu; JVM specification kosam designed ayindi.

steps.title: Inspect the JVM responsibilities before launch
steps.question: When `java` starts the class, several runtime stages occur before and during the call to `main`, including loading, verification, linking, initialization, interpretation or JIT compilation, and memory management. How do these JVM responsibilities connect the bytecode you just inspected to real execution?
steps.why: The JVM turns verified class-file bytecode into managed execution on the host machine.
steps.why_te: the JVM responsibilities before launch gurinchi definition memorize cheyyakunda source, compiler, bytecode, runtime flow lo ee screen ekkada fit avutundo environment evidence tho map cheskondi. JVM class file ni locate/load chesi verify chestundi, references link chestundi, class initialize chestundi, main invoke chestundi, bytecode ni interpret/JIT chestundi mariyu runtime memory ni manage chestundi.
